title: McKinsey: a third of companies skipped a SaaS purchase because agents can build it
subtitle: The 2026 State of AI survey finds 32% of organizations passed on at least one software product or feature after deciding agentic coding tools could produce it internally.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: McKinsey's 2026 State of AI global survey, circulating this week, reports that 32% of organizations have decided against buying at least one software product or feature because they could build it internally using agentic coding tools. It is the first year the survey has captured the build-versus-buy question as an AI story rather than an IT one, and the number is high enough to reshape planning at both ends of the transaction: the buyers who now consider a bespoke agent output the default option, and the vendors who used to count on the friction of building anything from scratch.

The mechanism is not that agents write all the code. It is that the ratio of prompt to shipped feature has collapsed inside internal engineering teams that have adopted Claude Code, Cursor, GitHub Copilot Workspace, or their equivalents. A category of tool that used to justify a six-figure annual contract — a lightweight admin dashboard, a data-transform utility, a middling reporting layer — now sits below the threshold where a team says 'yes, we'll build.' McKinsey pairs the finding with data showing that companies most aggressively rewiring their software delivery process around agents are the ones reporting the largest ROI from AI overall.

For the software industry the second-order effect is more interesting than the headline. Vendors selling into the crowded middle — enough value to justify a purchase order, not enough to be irreplaceable — are the ones getting squeezed. Vendors that own hard-to-replicate distribution (payments rails, regulated integrations, enterprise identity) or hard-to-replicate data are less exposed, because a build-with-agents team still cannot conjure a Visa contract or a decade of usage telemetry from a prompt.

Takeaway for learners: the useful question is not 'will AI kill SaaS?' It is 'which parts of a SaaS product cannot be produced by a competent team with an agent and a week?' If the answer is 'not much,' the price and moat both compress. If the answer is 'the integrations, the trust, the data, the compliance,' the vendor is fine and the price probably rises. Reading procurement outcomes through that lens tells you more about the shape of the enterprise-software market in 2027 than any benchmark chart will.
